The general idea here is that you want to frontload all of your "busy" activities to the start of the day and wake up early, tire yourself out by noon and then when you naturally shift to autopilot, do the stuff that isn't hard to do. For example, making a plan for the next day is a great thing to do in your evening. At the start of the day you're full of energy, so you overestimate what you can get done. At the end of the day, you're tired, so you give yourself plenty of time to get everything done, which in the end leaves you adding extra stuff to the list and coming out ahead. Checking the weather and laying out your clothes for the next day is also a good thing to do, because it's a waste of those precious first 15 minutes out of bed to spend it deciding what shirt you're going to wear. If its atrophied from lack of use over the years, using it will come difficultly, but over time it will grow stronger and can be used more effectively and longer before tiring. The more you use the "presence of mind" muscle, the more influence you'll exert over the rest of your life, the happier you'll be. A bit of presence of mind here to establish a morning routine, a bit there to improve your diet, a bit spent over there to educate yourself on a subject you were always interested in but lacked motivation for... In this metaphor, it may be hard to even perceive the soul at the center because of the "spiritual debris" cluttering the inner sanctum of your temple (that is to say, your mind and your neuroses). You might notice here that "presence of mind" as I've used it is almost a synonym for "free will", but I think it's more approachable as a concept for a non-theist to grasp... "Conscious thought"/"thinking consciously" is another very-related term that could be used for the same concept.

We're on autopilot most of the time, and only the most hardcore people can always be "in the moment", but capitalizing on the moments when you catch yourself not on autopilot is the trick to changing everything that bothers you.
